morning.title: Anthropic decides to support OpenAI's markdown instructions spec
morning.text: Anthropic on Friday surprised the developer community by supporting rival OpenAI's mechanism for passing marching orders to AI agents. This makes life easier for folks who use both platforms. "We're adding support for AGENTS.md to Claude Code," said Claude Code engineer Thariq Shihipar in a social media post. "Starting today in version 2.1.277, if there is no CLAUDE.md in a folder, Claude will check for and use AGENTS.md." Claude Code users can toggle this behavior, he said, with the /config command. Until now, developers who use Claude Code alongside OpenAI Codex or other non-Anthropic tools have had to maintain two sets of Markdown instructions for their AI agents: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, not to mention project-specific versions of these files. These documents get read by coding agents with every request. They outline expected behavior, preferred tool usage, coding conventions, and so on. They lay the foundation of the agent's context. The two formats are similar but not identical – CLAUDE.md may contain Claude-specific instructions while AGENTS.md is intended to be tool agnostic. Because these documents can change, those working with AI agents have implemented various workarounds, like creating symlinks to keep CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md in sync. Last year, OpenAI contributed AGENTS.md to the Agentic AI Foundation, under the Linux Foundation, in a bid to build support for its standard. As of December 2025, more than 60,000 open source projects implemented AGENTS.md. The popularity of Claude Code has given Anthropic the latitude to insist on its own standards, but it appears the company has decided there's nothing to be gained from continued specification separatism. For those who use AI coding tools, this detente is an event of modest significance. Many widely followed software developers applauded the decision in social media posts. Thibault Sottiaux, OpenAI's head of core product, remarked, "Yay! This is the way. Come to the light," to which Shihipar responded with the handshake emoji (🤝). It's enough to bring a tear to the eye. ®

morning.title: Microsoft agentically ports Copilot runtime to Rust for $120K
morning.text: The software engine underpinning GitHub Copilot and a growing number of Microsoft products is now written entirely in Rust, with AI agents doing most of the porting work. The migration cost about $120,000 in AI token usage plus about three weeks of a developer's time. However, managers also had to grapple with a few dozen regressions in the resulting code, pointing to AI’s ongoing challenges in understanding Rust. The effort updated the runtime module-by-module until the job was completed, spanning over 135 releases across a 14.5-week time period. Roughly 1.3 port pull requests were opened per day. Overall, agents converted 430,000 lines of TypeScript into 800,000 lines of production Rust. To keep the port as simple as possible, the port only replaced TypeScript modules on a case-by-case basis. It didn’t look to optimize the structure of the runtime itself. That work is next. And Rust, known for its lean performance, did not disappoint. One benchmark measured how quickly the runtime could complete 1,000 one-turn session lifecycles, using a shared client and 100 concurrent pipelines. The original TypeScript implementation completed 7.55 of those lifecycles per second, while Rust running in-process managed 120 per second - representing a 15.9x speedup on that particular workload. In terms of memory, a 10-client batch of agents consumed 1,383 MB with TypeScript while the Rust rewrite consumed only 126 MB serving the same swarm. Within Rust, the work remained in-process instead of spawning external background processes for completion, a requirement for TypeScript. Copilot from VS Code to Microsoft Office At first glance, most users may not know how pervasive the Copilot runtime is. It backs the GitHub Copilot command-line interface (CLI), the Copilot app, the SDK and the GitHub Copilot cloud agent. It shows up in VS Code, Visual Studio, Excel, Outlook, PowerPoint, and innumerable other Microsoft cloud services. Originally, the runtime was written in TypeScript and used Node.js as the framework and V8 for the execution engine. TypeScript and Node were ace for rapid development, but when used at scale, they suffered in terms of providing fast start-up and server density. “This is in no way a claim that every large TypeScript program should become Rust. Our requirements emphasized embedding through a C ABI, low startup and steady-state overhead, and predictable resource use. Rust made those goals possible,” wrote Microsoft Distinguished Engineer Stephen Toub in a post that explained the entire process. The project used Copilot to rewrite Copilot, which in turn used several LLMs – GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.8 were both namechecked – to execute different parts of the job, depending on each LLM’s natural strength. Well-read but chatty agents Toub assessed the use of agents as largely successful. Indeed, this project would have taken years and cost millions if done by hand. Agents showed several surprising emergent behaviors, Toub noted. For one, they spent far more time gathering information than actually writing code. “The popular image of AI spewing code is almost backwards; at this scale, the work looked much more like iterative investigation, inspecting the current state, forming a hypothesis, making a targeted change, rinsing and repeating,” he wrote. Another surprise was how frequently sessions interacted with other sessions, either those they spawned or other ones entirely. One of the thorniest conversions was the session.ts file, which was over 30,000 lines of TypeScript that touched all aspects of the runtime. The porting session, which ended up taking 25 hours to complete, began by spending 56 minutes reading the documentation and making 122 tool calls for clarification. It then spawned 15 child sessions, each creating its own worktree and agent. Then, they started communicating with each other. Using a built-in orchestration skill, one session found every other active session and sent messages to those whose missions overlapped, requesting coordination. The compiler is a teacher, not an oracle  Given its performance benefits, Rust has proven to be a popular language for rewriting applications. Bun creator Jarred Sumner, for instance, recently ported the Anthropic-owned JavaScript runtime and toolkit, which contained roughly 535,000 lines of Zig code, over to Rust, almost entirely using Claude agents. As of July 30, the experimental Rust port was passing 99.8 percent of Bun's existing tests on Linux x64 glibc, with the stable releases still shipping from the Zig codebase. That job cost $165,000 in tokens. But there are hidden dangers in using Rust as well, as Toub has found. For an LLM and a lazy programmer alike, if the code compiles, then it is valid Rust. But throughout the process, the project encountered dozens of regressions within the code. A regression is something that used to work, but no longer does after an update. The compiler has no idea, for instance, whether functions are in the right order, whether the job completes at an acceptable cost, whether it meets the developer's unwritten requirements, or whether it is internally coherent at all, for that matter. At RustConf, held in Montréal last week, consultant Lisa Crossman warned about the practice of treating the compiler as an “oracle,” or the last word on whether some Rust code is valid or not. “Rust stops the agent writing memory unsafe code; it does not stop the agent writing the wrong program correctly,” she said. If they’re wise, a human developer treats the compiler as a teacher, decoding the errors as a path to a better understanding of the language’s domain. An LLM, on the other hand, just uses the compiler as a black box, one it can batter with blunt, inefficient workarounds until one passes muster (perhaps this is what Zig creator Andrew Kelley meant when he called Bun’s Rust code “unreviewed slop”). In Toub’s case, he had found that compiler-approved regressions could come from ambiguous semantics and behaviors, branch drift, missing features that weren’t ported over, and differing behaviors from the replacement code. “That’s in no way an argument against Rust’s compiler,” Toub wrote. “But ‘if it compiles, it’s correct’ is useful only as a joke.” ®

morning.title: Virginia governor wakes up to fact datacenters have become political cancer
morning.text: Virginia is not just for lovers, but is also for datacenters, hosting more than anywhere else in the world. However, the growth could be slowing as Governor Abigail Spanberger issued an executive order on Friday cracking down on bit barn builds in the state. “In the years before I took office, datacenters came to Virginia and the Commonwealth did not have a clear or coordinated plan to address their impacts on Virginians … That changes today,” Spanberger said in a statement. The executive order is part of a broader datacenter accountability framework that calls for greater transparency, a ban on nondisclosure agreements, limits on permitting, and more stringent environmental controls. Spanberger argues that existing policy lacked the precision necessary to hold bit barn builders accountable, and that the order is necessary to protect residents. In addition to greater transparency, the broader framework would require local approval for datacenters exceeding 25 megawatts and remove future large datacenters from the expedited permitting process, while the order calls on government officials to establish criteria to distinguish between responsible datacenter developments and those that would negatively impact residents or the environment. Speaking of the environment, the order would limit the use of water-intensive cooling towers in areas suffering from water scarcity, and encourage datacenter operators to either retrofit existing backup generators to reduce emissions or switch to battery storage, fuel cells, and other clean energy sources. Friday's order comes just days after the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors backed a plan to pause final action on certain new datacenter and substation applications for up to 12 months. Loudoun County is home to one of the highest concentrations of datacenters in the state. Opposition to datacenter development across the US is on the rise amid growing concerns over the server farms' impact on air quality, noise pollution, water use, and residents' electric bills. In Tennessee, Elon Musk's Colossus 2 datacenter is powered in part by 27 gas turbines across the state line in Mississippi, which are now the subject of an NAACP lawsuit alleging violations of the Clean Air Act. Meanwhile, some states have gone even further and outright blocked the development of new datacenters while local governments get a better handle on their potential impacts. In July, New York became the first state to temporarily halt datacenter buildouts exceeding 50 megawatts as part of an executive order signed by Governor Kathy Hochul. A month later, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro issued an executive order blocking datacenter permit applications unless they made legally binding commitments to abide by the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development (GRID) requirements. Much like Virginia’s executive order, these rules seek to ensure residents don’t end up footing the bill for grid improvements built based on speculative demand. ®

morning.title: Compsci grads facing recession-like job prospects thanks to AI
morning.text: Thanks to AI, computer science majors are finding themselves in a tougher spot than they might have expected. Jobs are harder to come by, and more graduates are ending up in lower-paying sectors like retail and food service. That’s according to a new working paper by three US Census Bureau economists examining how college graduates from majors with the highest exposure to AI have fared since ChatGPT came onto the scene in late 2022 and helped kick off the generative AI boom. The results don’t look good for those in the most exposed fields, with career and earnings prospects for the top decile (i.e., the top ten percent of majors most exposed to AI) looking as bad as those of older Millennials who graduated during the Great Recession. “The most AI-exposed decile of college majors saw their likelihood of initial employment decline by five percentage points, while full-quarter initial earnings declined by 13 percent,” a trio of Census Bureau economists wrote in the paper. “This earnings decline is comparable in magnitude to the earnings losses associated with graduating into a large recession.” And why are those earnings declining? Well, part of the answer is where the AI-affected graduates are ending up: With job prospects worsening, more are turning to lower-wage sectors like restaurants and retail, with the researchers finding that shifts into lower-paying industries account for about half of the earnings decline. The one big difference between your usual recession and what’s happening now, the economists explain, is that the effects aren’t spread evenly across all industries. Graduates from less AI-exposed fields, including nursing and many education fields, haven’t experienced the same deterioration in early-career employment seen among those from the most exposed majors. Those having trouble are largely who you’d think: Graduates in computer science, mathematics, statistics, some engineering disciplines, networking, and (gulp) even journalists are among those in the most AI-exposed fields. The impacts that young graduates are feeling have tended to ease as they move further from graduation, but previous research on those who entered the workforce around the Great Recession suggests that years of lousy job prospects can leave graduates behind the curve on earnings. The researchers acknowledge that other factors could be at play, but the paper finds that several alternative explanations don’t fully account for the pattern. Is there an oversupply of new graduates in those fields, given how popular they are? Probably not, the paper notes, and the authors explained to us. “The most AI-exposed majors saw rapid growth in graduates in the years leading up to ChatGPT's release. After its release, the number of new graduates in these majors started to level off quickly,” the authors explained in an email to The Register. “Survey data on STEM departments also suggest that enrollments in some of the most exposed major programs have started to decline.” That said, the number of those graduates who found jobs in their field has fallen faster, they added. What about self-employment or the grad school route? Together, changes in those activities could account for as much as half of the five-percentage-point employment decline, the paper concludes. In other words, AI appears to be having an impact on the job market for young people, especially those in the most AI-exposed fields, though other factors are at play. “There are many different plausible ways in which AI may be impacting early career workers,” the research team told us. “Firms may have chosen to hire fewer new graduates for reasons that are related to AI's existence, but aren't related to firms' use of the technology themselves.” Those who aren’t embracing AI in their business may simply be less certain about the future, or they may be concerned that AI is making it harder to find suitable candidates, both of which can make job prospects for fresh graduates worse, the economists told us. The takeaway from the entire paper is essentially that, yes, AI is reshaping the labor market, and it’s having a disproportionate impact on young folks who went to school to do jobs that are being affected by AI, like software development and writing. “We should be concerned about the magnitude of these results,” the researchers told us, but they added that they hesitate to extrapolate this short-term trend into a long-term doomsday forecast for the future of the labor market. “Historical evidence shows that many jobs performed today did not exist decades ago, and it's not easy to predict what those jobs of the future might be or what skills they may require,” the authors told us. “We should be very cautious in speculating about how AI will impact the economy as a whole based on shorter-term effects on only a subset of workers.” Still, the evidence to date suggests new compsci graduates fielding questions from their parents about why they’re still slinging frappuccinos or waiting tables have a ready answer: It’s all AI’s fault. ®

morning.title: Claude Code revamps projects so you can work and pay in parallel
morning.text: Claude Code customers have a new reason to give Anthropic more of their money. The tool now allows you to launch multiple sessions related to a single project, burning through more resources and cash at once. Appropriately enough, the feature is called projects and can be accessed from the Claude.ai sidebar. It's not the old version of projects, capitalized in some reference material, which allowed for the creation of self-contained workspaces with separate chat histories and knowledge bases. The new implementation is technically in beta, though that term hardly means anything anymore amid the constant code iteration. Anthropic describes projects as a way to let Claude manage multiple related tasks. "Claude scopes the request, delegates the work, coordinates parallel threads, reviews the outputs, and assembles the finished result," the company explains in a blog post. "You can steer progress throughout, even from your phone, and it keeps working after you step away from your computer." It's the sort of capability that might be useful if you are prompting the model to begin a large coding project and you want to get several essential components like authorization, databases, caching, and containers up and running at the same time. Essentially, a project spins up each task as its own Claude Code cloud session thread that works on its own git branch and its own copy of the relevant repo. A coordinator directs the threads; if they touch the same code, overlaps surface as merge conflicts like those in other pull requests. And each thread may get broken down into distinct tasks handled by subagents within that session. Claude Code now offers five different ways to run multiple tasks at the same time. Subagents work within a session, though each with its own context. Agent View provides a single screen interface for overseeing several independent tasks. Agent Teams allows coordinating multiple Claude Code instances that can share information and communicate. Dynamic Workflows allows subagents to be orchestrated by a script. And then there's projects, intended for work that spans multiple repositories, migrations that require more than a single session, or work that isn't code, like a frequently queried set of support tickets or documentation. Anthropic's caveat is that projects burn through tokens quickly. "Projects can run several threads at once, and each one is a full Claude Code session," the company explains. "Because of this, projects can reach usage limits faster." Select Pro and Max subscribers should have access to the Projects beta so long as they use Claude Code and don't have existing Projects set up on web or desktop. Pro and Max users without access can join a waitlist as Anthropic gradually expands the rollout. Team and Enterprise plans don't have access to the redesigned Projects beta yet. Anthropic reportedly told investors that, in its second quarter, it posted an adjusted operating profit - if you don't count expenses including stock-based compensation. Q2 revenue is said to be $11.5 billion, and if enough customers create projects that run multiple Claude Code threads at once, that figure could be higher still. ®

morning.title: Finding the cells that put our brain to sleep
morning.text:
For a long time, sleep research has treated the cerebral cortex as a passive follower reacting to signals from the deep brain. “Usually, sleep is associated with being controlled by subcortical regions,” said Geoffrey Terral, a neuroscientist at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York.

The cortex is where the slow rhythms of deep sleep can be seen, but researchers assumed the signals that triggered them originated elsewhere. In a recent Nature study, Terral and Renata Batista-Brito, who runs the lab, report a population of cortical cells that challenges that assumption.

These cortical cells make up only around one percent of the cortex's inhibitory neurons, and switching them on in a mouse puts the animal to sleep. “What our work shows is that the cortex can not only see this rhythm but also initiate it by itself, and this is sufficient to promote sleep,” Terral said.

morning.title: Researchers used Claude to hack OpenAI employees' ChatGPT accounts
morning.text: Talk about your competitor getting through the door. Security researchers used Anthropic's Claude to help hack into OpenAI employees’ ChatGPT accounts. A trio of bug hunters researching frontier AI labs’ security weaknesses chained two vulnerabilities to take over multiple OpenAI employees’ ChatGPT accounts, then used that access to demonstrate they could reach an internal OpenAI repository by opening a harmless pull request. The entire timeline, from initial discovery to accessing OpenAI’s repo, took less than 72 hours and earned the researchers a $6,500 reward from OpenAI’s bug bounty program on Bugcrowd. “Until two months ago, any user or OpenAI employee logging into OpenAI’s own help forum (community.openai.com) could have had their ChatGPT and Codex accounts taken over,” Hacktron researchers Harsh Jaiswal, Mohan Pedhapati, and Rahul Maini said in a writeup about their research. “Since people can connect various services to Codex and ChatGPT, the scope of what we could theoretically access was huge, including GitHub, Slack and emails.” And, in a poetic twist, they used rival AI giant Anthropic’s Claude models to develop the exploit. Claude has shown a propensity to hack organizations without human guidance, as have OpenAI's models. The team gained initial entry on July 25 via OpenAI’s community forum. The forum runs on Discourse, which typically uses FastImage to perform image checks. However, since FastImage didn’t support HEIF files in the affected setup, HEIF images uploaded to Discourse passed through ImageMagick, which used libheif to process them before converting them to another image format. “That exposed the underlying libheif parser directly to attacker-controlled files,” the researchers wrote. Using Claude Opus 4.8, the trio found a heap buffer overflow flaw in the libheif library and attempted to use that model to develop a remote code execution (RCE) attack, but this didn’t work on Discourse’s default configuration. But then, Anthropic released Claude Opus 5. The bug hunters used the newer model to generate an exploit script, and achieved RCE on OpenAI’s instance. The trio “immediately” reported the vulnerability to OpenAI. “We then took over an OpenAI employee’s account, whose Codex was connected to OpenAI’s Github organization,” they wrote. “To demonstrate impact without actually accessing any internal code, we sent a prompt to this employee’s Codex account to open a PR for us in OpenAI’s internal monorepo. Then we stopped any further testing.” Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic responded to The Register’s requests for comment. OpenAI fixed the flaw within about 14 hours of the report’s submission, marked the issue as resolved, and paid the Hacktron team a $6,500 bounty. “To clarify the scope of that award: testing against the Discourse-hosted community.openai.com was explicitly excluded from our bug bounty program,” OpenAI said in a comment shared by Hacktron. “The award recognizes the OpenAI-side finding, not the actions against Discourse.” Discourse also issued a fix that added image-processing sandboxing, and published a security advisory GHSA-vhm9-85gw-x335 with patching and rebuild guidance. The entire hack took a few days for an AI agent and a few hours of human work. “Work that once required a well-resourced team and months of effort can now be compressed into days,” the researchers said. “Security assumptions must catch up with attacker capabilities.” ®

morning.title: Pakistan signs interceptor drone deal with Trump family-backed Powerus
morning.text:
New Delhi: To enhance its drone capabilities, Pakistan has signed a defence deal with Trump-backed Powerus, a US based drone company known for its Guardian series interceptor drones.
Pakistan’s interest in Powerus follows the four-day skirmish with India in May 2025, the first instance in which both countries used drones as strike weapons. India used drones for reconnaissance, surveillance and precision strikes.
Islamabad is reportedly considering purchasing Powerus’s Guardian Interceptor line, designed to counter one-way attack drones. The company backed by two sons of US President Donald Trump produces about 3,000 drone interceptors a month, priced at roughly $5,000 a piece, according to a Financial Times (FT) report. It began manufacturing interceptors in the UAE this June amid the West Asia conflict.
“Powerus has received a limited procurement order from the Ministry of Defence of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan for unmanned aerial systems and associated support. The order represents an expansion of our international defense business,” a press release by Powerus stated Thursday.
Powerus’ interceptor family, according to its website, has evolved across three generations: Guardian 1 (manual origins), Guardian-2 (semi-autonomous operation): and Guardian-3 (fire-and-forget ecosystem):
“We have also signed a strategic MoU with senior defense officials of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan. It sets a framework for potential expanded cooperation in unmanned and autonomous systems, subject to definitive agreements and government approvals,” the release added.
Powerus has received a limited procurement order from the Ministry of Defence of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan for unmanned aerial systems and associated support. The order represents an expansion of our international defense business.

Andrew Fox, the company’s founder and chief executive, dubbed Pakistan’s private defense sector as “emerging but still not mature,” leaving an opening for American firms.
In an interview to Reuters, he said the two sides are aiming for a mutual arrangement that pairs American and Pakistani technology, with Powerus also weighing whether to manufacture equipment inside Pakistan.
Pakistan’s military said, in a statement, that a Powerus delegation led by Velicovich met Field Marshal Asim Munir, to discuss defence procurement, production and long-term capacity-building. Their statement, however, made no mention of the MoU.
China has been Pakistan’s biggest defence exporter with Beijing accounting for 80% of military acquisitions between 2021 and 2025, valued at approximately $5.28 billion, according to a 2025 SIPRI report.
Munir is seeking to capitalise on the growing US-Pakistan relationship. The defence deal comes after deals in crypto and critical minerals. In January, Islamabad signed an MoU with Trump-backed World Liberty Financial, a crypto company co-founded by Zach Witkoff, the son of US special envoy and close Trump aide Steve Witkoff.
“Pakistan has the opportunity not only diplomatically but economically, to create industry here, create jobs, and create export opportunities. This is more than a one-off for us. This is the establishment of a long-term relationship,” Fox told FT after the deal.
Similarly, Powerus president and co-founder Brett Velicovich told FT that the US had for decades avoided providing drone systems to countries such as Pakistan, while China supplied them more freely. He said this created a dependence on China, but US policy is now changing, with Washington becoming more willing to share its drone technology with other countries.
Currently, the Chinese origin CH-4 and Wing Loong II as well as the Bayraktar, the Byker Yiha Kamikaze, and the Asisguard Songar from Turkey are part of the Pakistani military’s drone fleet.
The Trump connection
The American defense and autonomy company is set to merge with Aureus Greenway Holdings in October. Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump hold a stake in Aureus through an investment fund called American Ventures, according to securities filings, which project the fund will retain roughly a 9.9 percent beneficial stake in the merged entity.
The combined entity would take the Powerus name and trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker ‘PUSA.’
Instead of taking a traditional IPO (where a private company raises capital to become a public trading corporation and be listed on the NSE or NASDAQ), Powerus is reportedly executing a reverse merger using Aureus Greenway Holdings, a publicly listed golf course operator where the Trump brothers are passive investors.
The brothers’ investment bank, Dominari Securities, has also played a role in raising capital for the deal, and the drone-parts supplier Unusual Machines, where Donald Trump Jr. sits on an advisory board is among the investors as well.
Fox is slated to become the CEO and chairperson of the unified Powerus Corporation.
Powerus is third investment of the Trump siblings in the drone sector after a $1.5 bn February tie-up with Israeli drone maker XTEND and Florida-based JFB Construction Holdings.

Satellite images show Iran rebuilding nuclear weapons site Taleghan 2 hit twice by Israel
morning.text:
New Delhi: High-resolution satellite imagery from Vantor Technologies shows Iran was reconstructing the destroyed nuclear testing site Taleghan 2 in June-July this year.
The site was struck twice by the Israeli military over the course of two major conflict periods.
Located in the Parchin Military Complex about 30 km southeast of Tehran, the facility was built in 2000 under the AMAD programme to advance Iran’s nuclear weapon design capabilities. While Iran officially suspended structured weaponisation activities in late 2003, watchdogs have monitored the site for covert research.
Situated on a campus which houses the different research processes for creating nuclear bombs, this particular site was designed to diagnose and test weapons capabilities, with the intention of weaponising research from other Iranian nuclear sites.
The first strike on the site was in October 2024, when the Israeli military conducted an aerial counterstrike against Iran, destroying the original Taleghan 2 building and specialised equipment used for nuclear weapons development.
The second strike was in March 2026. After a year spent rebuilding and fortifying the site inside a concrete, coffin-like superstructure buried under the Earth, Israeli forces hit it again using heavy bunker-buster munitions to penetrate the new underground structure. A defensive wall in the front collapsed from an internal blast, the shockwave destroying a support building outside.
Later, between 24 March and 1 April 2026, a fire control and instrument building—part of the Taleghan 1 structure—was hit along with the facility’s nearby headquarters building.
An analysis by the Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS) of the images provided by Vantor Technologies via CNN shows reconstruction efforts starting in mid-June.
On 12 June, images show the three locations that were hit were covered, along with a makeshift path to establish ground-level access, as most routes were rendered unusable—especially on the northern side.
Days later, on 18 June, vehicles including several trucks and a large crane were spotted south of the site.
Images from 20 June show rubble being cleared from the headquarters building which stood nearby, before the second phase of the March 2026 raids.
Images from between 22 June and 7 July show Iran’s attempts to permanently cover the holes. The area around the holes had been excavated, cleared, and covered with screening material, which was removed by 7 July. In the 22 June images, workers can be seen pouring concrete to reinforce the facility’s southeast corner.
The images from 7 July also show that the area around the holes was cleared to create further access, while a crane worked directly at the impact zones. Other indicators, such as a mesh, were placed over the area to reinforce the concrete that will eventually be poured over it.
These activities in Iran suggest that the area will be buried under dirt to place the facility underground.
A broader look at Parchin shows debris piles from cleanup and removal efforts at destroyed missile production facilities near Taleghan 2 in May 2026.
(Edited by Viny Mishra)

morning.title: India rejects Pakistan’s allegations on ship collision in high seas, underlines PNS Hunain was at fault
morning.text:
New Delhi: India Friday rejected Pakistan’s allegations on the alarming incident in the high seas where a Pakistani naval ship dangerously collided with INS Kolkata earlier this week.
Islamabad sought to blame the INS Kolkata for the incident, and lodged a protest with New Delhi. Randhir Jaiswal, the official spokesperson for the Ministry of External Affairs, underlined that the Indian naval ship was on “routine deployment” before the PNS Hunain “conducted itself in an unacceptable and unprofessional manner” that resulted in the collision.
“We have seen Pakistan’s response to the protest we had lodged. It is the usual prevarication that we expected. We reject the allegations and insinuations contained therein,” Jaiswal said at a regular press briefing.
He added: “The dangerous overtaking manoeuvre by PNS Hunain was in gross violation of Article 10 of the Agreement between India and Pakistan on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements of April 1991, which specifies that naval units at sea are not to be within 3 nautical miles of each other. In addition, the Pakistani ship also infringed the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea.”
India urged Pakistan to ensure all military units “observe due care” and respect the existing agreements in place between both countries to manage such situations. The INS Kolkata continued with her deployment, and is currently at sea.
The incident occurred late Tuesday evening in the North Arabian Sea, when the PNS Hunain collided dangerously with the INS Kolkata. The Pakistani naval ship, built by Damen Shipyards in Romania, was commissioned in July 2024.
The INS Kolkata issued warnings to the approaching Pakistani vessel. Towards the end of the encounter, the PNS Hunain attempted a close-range manoeuvre, which resulted in the collision, as reported by ThePrint.
The Pakistani vessel suffered a dent, and potentially even a crack, thereby being forced to return to harbour. The PNS Hunain was unable to steer clear of the Indian vessel. The Yarmook-class vessel was part of an ongoing Pakistani military exercise in the area, according to the statement issued by Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Despite the reported exercise—SEASPARK-26—ongoing at the time, the area where the collision occurred was not designated as a “no-go area” as reported by ThePrint.
The INS Kolkata was operationally deployed in the region to escort commercial ships coming through the Gulf of Oman, as the security situation in West Asia continues to deteriorate.
The PNS Hunain is a multipurpose off-shore patrol vessel, and can accommodate a helicopter and unmanned aerial systems, besides a 60-member crew. The PNS Hunain is the third vessel of the Yarmook-class to be commissioned by the Pakistani Navy.
(Edited by Gitanjali Das)

morning.title: Meet the winner of Nikon's Small World in Motion video contest
morning.text:
A Chinese optical engineer is the winner of this year's Small World in Motion competition, sponsored by Nikon. Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in Beijing beat out 346 other video entries from 40 different countries with his super-resolution video (above) of the abnormal beating of cilia in the airways of a child with a rare genetic respiratory disorder.

Founded in 2011, the Nikon Small World in Motion competition is a spinoff of the company's Small World Photomicrography Competition, which has been around since 1974. Both are meant "to showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the light microscope"—one through still photographs, the other through photovideography, taking advantage of all the technological advances that now allow users to make movies or time-lapse images through the microscope.

Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is a genetic disorder that adversely affects the tiny hairlike structures that line the lungs, among other areas. Their wavelike motion helps move around germs, mucus, dust, and other irritants so the body can dispel them via coughing or sneezing. In people born with PCD, there is something wrong with those cilia, so those irritants build up, causing respiratory infections, among other complications. The cilia might be the wrong size, the wrong shape, or missing altogether. They might move abnormally or not move at all.

morning.title: HAL hands over final two Tejas Mk1 trainers 16 years after IAF order, all eyes on Mk1A now
morning.text:
New Delhi: Sixteen years after the Indian Air Force (IAF) placed an order, state-run Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) has finally handed over the last two Tejas trainer aircraft from the original Mk1 programme. This closes an order that was meant to have been completed nearly a decade ago.
The two trainers, in Final Operational Clearance (FOC) configuration, were handed over in the presence of Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and IAF Chief of Air Staff Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh.
The delivery completes the two separate Tejas Mk1 orders placed by the IAF in 2006 and 2010. On 31 March 2006, the IAF ordered 20 Tejas Mk1 aircraft in Initial Operational Clearance (IOC) configuration, comprising 16 fighters and four trainers. Deliveries were to be completed by December 2011.
On 23 December 2010, another 20 Mk1 aircraft were ordered in FOC configuration, comprising 16 fighters and four trainers. The contractual deadline for this order was December 2016.
Defence establishment sources said the fundamental problem behind the delay was that the aircraft’s development and certification lagged behind production contracts. IOC, originally expected around 2008, was achieved only in December 2013, while the first IOC-standard fighter was delivered in 2016-17.
The FOC version faced further delays because of air-to-air refuelling integration, structural modifications, flight-control software changes and associated testing. Sources said the IAF was clear that the remaining trainers would be accepted only after the required safety, structural and performance issues had been addressed.
With the original 40-aircraft order finally completed, attention now shifts to the much larger Tejas Mk1A programme. The IAF ordered 83 Mk1As, 73 fighters and 10 trainers, from HAL in 2021 for about Rs 48,000 crore. Under the contract, the first aircraft was to be delivered within three years, by February 2024, with the entire order to be completed over nine years.
ThePrint had reported then that one of the primary worries for the IAF was whether HAL will deliver on time or not.
But the first Mk1A, LA-5033, made its maiden flight from HAL’s Bengaluru facility only in March 2024. Two-and-a-half years later, HAL is yet to hand over a single aircraft to the IAF.
The IAF has not accepted the aircraft, pending completion and validation of key systems, including radar, weapons and electronic-warfare capabilities. HAL has given several timelines for beginning deliveries over the past two years, but has missed them.
While the shortage of GE F404 engines has emerged as a major bottleneck, the programme also has outstanding software, systems-integration and testing requirements. Over the last two years, HAL has given several delivery dates to the IAF, promising to finish the pending works but failed.
The IAF has actually compromised on several key promises made by HAL.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh had taken a review meeting in June this year, and was of the view that HAL should sit down with the IAF and come up with a reasonable timeline, and that it should not overpromise and under-deliver.
With HAL getting a new Chairman and Managing Director, Ravi Kota, known as ‘LCA man’ within defence circles, the IAF is hopeful of HAL managing to turn things around. Contrary to the previous two CMDs, the HAL chairman in his interactions with journalists has admitted to delays and offered a more realistic time to finish off the pending work.
He estimates that the Mk1A programme is around 90-95 percent complete. “There are a few radar issues, and weapon integration is done. There have to be some tests for confirming standards. It’s only the software change, that’s all. But, having said that, when you put a missile, you need to go, bang, go up and come down. How the missile or the structure will behave – all those tests are required. It’s a process that has to be followed,” he told The Hindu Business Line.
Kota has said HAL has so far received 10 GE F404 engines, with another 12 promised by December, and that the company hopes to begin Mk1A deliveries by the end of the current financial year.
ThePrint has consistently reported that contrary to the popular perception and claims by the previous two CMDs of HAL, there are several other significant issues with the Tejas which HAL has not been able to address.
(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

morning.title: What is Dive-LD, America’s ‘most modern submersible’ that Iran claims to have captured near Hormuz
morning.text:
New Delhi: The Iranian Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said on Tuesday that it captured one of the US’ “most modern” underwater drones near the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian state media identified the vessel as a Dive-LD, a large autonomous underwater vehicle manufactured by Anduril, a California-based defence technology company.
The roughly 19-foot (5.8 meters) unmanned submersible is designed for missions including mine countermeasures, seabed mapping, intelligence gathering and the inspection of underwater infrastructure such as cables and pipelines.
“One of the US military’s most advanced unmanned underwater vehicles was seized by Iranian forces near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC Navy said.
Purported images of the submersible released later showed a partially submerged, cylindrical gray-and-white vessel bearing Anduril markings and US Navy serial identifiers consistent with the platform’s known design.
The Pentagon, however, disputed the characterisation of the incident as a military capture. A spokesman for the US Central Command said the underwater drone had malfunctioned over a day before the Iranian announcement and had effectively been disabled in the water.
“The drone was essentially dead in the water for more than a day. It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations,” US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins told Defensescoop, a Washington-based news outlet covering US military acquisitions. He also said the vehicle was an older model that “neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment.”
Anduril confirmed that one of its Dive-LD vehicles had been lost but downplayed the incident. The company described the Dive-LD as an “attritable autonomous system,” meaning that it is designed to operate in hazardous environments where the loss of a vehicle is considered an acceptable possibility.
“Its purpose is to keep warfighters out of the most dangerous parts of the undersea mission,” an Anduril spokesman said, adding that the vehicle had accumulated thousands of hours of operations in the US Central Command area. Unlike conventional submarines, these systems can conduct extended missions without putting crews at risk.
Enhanced capabilities
According to Anduril’s website, the Dive-LD is 1.2 meters in diameter and weighs roughly three tons. It can remain at sea for extended periods and is designed to operate at depths of up to 6,000 meters. The company has also said that the vehicle’s open mechanical, electrical and software interfaces, allow different sensors and payloads to be integrated for specific missions.
The vehicle can be configured for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, mine warfare and what Anduril describes as “precision placement.” Its modular design has also raised the possibility of variants eventually carrying a broader range of military payloads, although there is no public evidence that the particular vehicle Iran displayed was armed.
Dive-LD vehicles are known to have entered US Navy service in April 2025, including with units responsible for unmanned undersea operations. The US Navy is also pursuing larger autonomous underwater systems, including Anduril’s Dive-XL, as part of a broader effort to expand its undersea capabilities.
Can Iran obtain data from the vessel?
According to Iranian media, an intact underwater vehicle could provide far more intelligence than a damaged or destroyed wreck and Iranian engineers could potentially examine the pressure hull’s materials and manufacturing tolerances, disassemble the battery system to study its cell chemistry, packaging and energy density, and inspect the propulsion system and control-surface actuators for engineering techniques aimed at reducing noise.
The most valuable information, however, could lie inside the vehicle’s electronics. If its data storage and onboard computing systems were not remotely erased, physically damaged or protected by anti-tamper mechanisms before the capture, they could potentially offer insights into the autonomy software, navigation algorithms and mission-planning systems that allow the vehicle to operate with limited or no human intervention.
The vehicle’s onboard memory could also contain detailed underwater data gathered during its mission, including high-resolution maps of the seabed.
Iran already maintains extensive charts of the waters on its side of the Strait of Hormuz. But data collected by the Dive-LD could potentially include surveys of the Omani side of the strait, as well as deep-water approaches and underwater terrain that Iranian forces have historically had less visibility into, according to reports.
Such information could give Iranian naval planners a more detailed picture of seabed contours, depth profiles and underwater obstacles across a strategically important waterway.
For Iran, which has been developing its own unmanned underwater systems, access to an intact Dive-LD could also offer a shortcut through years of research and development. Reverse engineering would not allow engineers to simply reproduce the vehicle, but studying its components could reveal solutions to some of the hardest problems in autonomous undersea operations, including surviving extreme water pressure, reducing acoustic signatures, managing power over long missions and maintaining accurate navigation without GPS.
(Edited by Chingkheinganbi Mayengbam)
